blocks.title: The school surplus

paragraphs.text: Tuition missed both ways: private schools came in $522,629 under budget, collaboratives $434,108 over.
Outside tuition, lines under budget left $815,327 and lines over budget took $421,731.
Some spending did not recur: 29 vendors paid in both years before were paid $361,639 less, net of every other route.
Tuition, across both funds, rose every year: $799,715 in FY2023, $1,536,266 in FY2026.
Two entries on 29 June and 30 June made the surplus smaller, by $333,495 and $189,277.
There is no deficit: what was left returns to the town’s general fund.

spec.title: What the surplus is made of

paragraphs.text: **Tuition for students placed outside Lunenburg’s schools missed its budget badly, in both directions.** Private special education schools were budgeted at $988,630 and cost $466,001: $522,629 under, 53%. Collaboratives (programs run jointly by several districts) were budgeted at $302,663 and the school budget paid $736,770: $434,108 over, 143%. Each is its own miss; no transfer covered one with the other.

**Outside tuition, the kinds of spending that finished under left $815,327, and the ones that ran over took $421,731.** Building upkeep left $195,934, counselors and psychologists $191,162 and teachers $167,992; paraprofessionals, special education contracted services and transportation ran over.

**Part of both staff figures is money moved between funds.** Journal reclasses moved $135,062 of teacher cost from the general fund to other school funds, and $205,645 of paraprofessional cost onto it; without those moves teachers left $32,931 and paraprofessionals ran $2,437 over. The journal shows the moves, not why they were made.

**What the budget assumed, and the ledger does not show.** All 6 kinds of spending that left the most were budgeted above what they spent the year before, and 3 then spent less again; building upkeep was budgeted 33.9% above its FY2025 spending. A psychologist account and a social worker account posted no payroll in months that paid $142,423 the year before, and 29 vendors paid in both of the two years before were paid $361,639 less, after every other route the money could have taken. Why is an open question; what would answer it: the payroll by position and date, which separates a post left vacant from every other cause, and the year’s grant award records.

**Tuition costs more every year.** It is paid from two places: the school budget, and the circuit breaker, the state’s reimbursement for high-cost special education. Counting both, it rose from $799,715 in FY2023 to $1,054,804, $1,205,949 and $1,536,266 in FY2026. The circuit breaker paid none of the private school tuition in FY2026, after paying 40–80% of it in each of the three years before.

**Two accounting entries in the year’s last two days both made the surplus smaller.** On 29 June, $333,495 of collaborative tuition already charged to the school budget was moved onto the circuit breaker, where the budget had planned $480,204; the Town Manager questioned it in writing, and it still stood on 6 October. On 30 June, $189,277 of next year’s (FY2027) tuition bills were charged to FY2026 and paid in July. FY2027 budgets this tuition at $700,142; FY2026 spent $1,346,989 on it, not counting the bills paid early.
**There is no deficit.** The school budget as a whole stayed under, and what was left returns to the town’s general fund. The town’s own departments closed FY2026 $964,030 under budget.
